pages.title: Welcome!
pages.content:
Welcome to the course on Learning Java for Development and Project building!

What will you learn here?
- All the basic concepts of Java programming language like - `Variables, Strings, Conditions, Lists, Loops, Methods and Basic OOP, File handling` etc
- By the end of this course, you will be able to write code in Java to Build real world projects
 - Basic projects and applications such as Command line calendar, File encryption tool, URL shortener
 - Data processing / File based projects such as CSV data analyzer, JSON data processor, PDF Text extractor 


Let the fun begin!

**Click on Next on the right to start**.

pages.title: Learning elements
pages.content:
You will come across the following learning elements in each concept in this course.

1. **Text Explanation:** Learn the concept through clear explanations, real-world applications, code snippets, and important tips.
2. **Visualizer:** See how code runs step-by-step instead of just the final output. \
This will help you understand how the code works and is very important for beginners.

Experiment with the code to deepen your understanding.

Think of these as the "Boss Level" for each concept!

pages.title: Getting Started
pages.content:
We are getting started with Java! Let's begin by greeting the world and learning how to write "Hello, World!" in Java. This will be our first program, and through it, we'll explore the basics of Java syntax..

Once we see our message printed, we'll break it down step by step, understanding its components, how Java processes it, and how we compile and run the program. This will set the foundation for everything we'll learn in Java!

---

**Example**

```java
System.out.println("Hello, World!"); // Printing a message to the console
```

Output:
```default
Hello, World!
```

---

 
 Fun Fact: 
 Java was initially named Oak after an oak tree outside the office of James Gosling, the creator of Java. Later, it was renamed Java, inspired by Java coffee.

pages.title: Statements and Semicolons in Java
pages.content:
In this lesson, you'll learn about statements in Java. A statement is a fundamental unit of execution that tells the computer to perform a specific action, much like a sentence in human language. Statements form the building blocks of any Java program, guiding the flow of execution step by step.

Most Java statements end with a semicolon (;), which acts like a full stop, marking the end of a command. While each statement is usually placed on a new line for readability, it is not strictly required.

---

**Example**

```java
System.out.println("Hello, World!"); // Printing a message to the console
```

Output:
```default
Hello, World!
```

---

By mastering Java statements and semicolon usage, you're taking the first step toward writing well-structured Java programs!

pages.title: Case Sensitivity in Java
pages.content:
In Java, case sensitivity is a fundamental concept that affects how the language interprets `method` names, `class` names, and `keywords`. Java distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters, meaning even slight differences in capitalization create separate identifiers.

When writing Java code, it's crucial to pay attention to the case of each character. A single misplaced uppercase or lowercase letter can lead to errors or unexpected behavior in your program.

pages.title: Comments in Java
pages.content:
In Java, comments are non-executable text added to improve code readability. They help explain the purpose of the code and are ignored by the compiler.

Remember, good comments explain why something is done, not just what is being done. Use comments to clarify complex logic, explain important decisions, or provide context that isn't immediately obvious from the code itself. 

---

**Java supports three types of comments**

1. **Single-line comments**
These start with // and are used for brief explanations.
```java
// This is a single-line comment
System.out.println("Hello, World!");
```

2. **Multi-line comments**
These start with /* and end with */, allowing longer explanations across multiple lines.
```java
/* This is a multi-line comment
 It can span multiple lines */
System.out.println("Hello, World!");
```

3. **Javadoc comments**
These special comments, starting with /** and ending with */, are used to generate documentation.
```java
/**
 * This is a Javadoc comment.
 * It describes a class, method, or interface.
 */
System.out.println("Hello, World!");
```

pages.title: How to Print a Message in Java
pages.content:
In Java, printing messages to the console is one of the most basic yet essential programming tasks. The `System.out.print` and `System.out.println()` method is used to display output and is readily available in Java without any additional imports.

**Syntax**
```java
System.out.print("Hello"); // Prints text but stays on the same line.
System.out.println(" World!"); // Prints text and moves to the next line.
```

---


1. **Printing Text**

To print words, enclose them in double quotes (`""`)
```java
// Using println() for a new line
System.out.println("Hello, World!"); // Output: Hello, World!
// Using print() to stay on the same line
System.out.print("Welcome to Java!"); // Output: Welcome to Java!
```

2. **Printing Numbers**

To print numbers, write them without quotes:
```java
// This prints a whole number
System.out.println(123); // Output: 123
// This prints a decimal number 
System.out.println(3.14); // Output: 3.14
```

pages.title: Introduction - Error and Exception Handling
pages.content: Exceptions represent conditions that interrupt normal program flow. Java uses `try` and `catch` to handle exceptions and prevent an expected failure from terminating the program unexpectedly.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Use exception handling to keep expected failures under control.

checkpoint.question: What is an exception in Java?

A variable declaration
A package name
A loop counter

pages.content: Different exceptions represent different failure conditions. Examples include `ArithmeticException`, `NumberFormatException`, and `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

Modern Java Type Modeling: Records, Enums and Sealed Types becomes useful when Java code needs to express a stable rule rather than a one-off syntax trick. **Learning focus**

- **canonical constructor** — understand the rule and when it belongs in a production design.
- **enum** — understand the rule and when it belongs in a production design.

pages.title: API anatomy and design rules
pages.content:
### API anatomy

A production learner should know not just *what* an API call does, but what contract surrounds it. For **Modern Java Type Modeling: Records, Enums and Sealed Types**, pay attention to:

1. **Inputs and types:** what values are accepted?
2. **State:** what data is owned or shared?
3. **Failure modes:** which errors are compile-time, runtime, or domain failures?
4. **Lifetime:** what must be closed, awaited, copied, or released?
5. **Observability:** how can you prove the operation produced the correct result?

**Design rule:** prefer the narrowest abstraction that expresses the contract. Expose stable interfaces and value objects at boundaries; keep mutable implementation details private.

pages.title: Debugging and failure analysis
pages.content:
### Debugging Modern Java Type Modeling: Records, Enums and Sealed Types

When a program fails, classify the failure before changing code:

**Compile-time:** the type or API contract is invalid.

**Runtime:** the program reaches an operation whose preconditions are violated.

**Logic:** the program runs but produces an incorrect state or output.

**Concurrency / lifecycle:** the code is valid in isolation but fails because timing, ownership, cleanup, or shared state was handled incorrectly.

- **Using records for mutable aggregates:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Treating enums as strings everywhere:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Making sealed hierarchies wider than the domain requires:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Assuming records replace every Java class:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.

**Debugging loop:** reproduce -> isolate -> state the rule -> fix one cause -> rerun the smallest failing case.

**Logic:** the program runs but produces an incorrect state or output.

**Concurrency / lifecycle:** the code is valid in isolation but fails because timing, ownership, cleanup, or shared state was handled incorrectly.

- **Treating GC as manual memory management:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Assuming System.gc guarantees collection:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Timing one tiny operation once:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Optimizing without measuring:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Confusing memory leak with high allocation rate:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.

**Debugging loop:** reproduce -> isolate -> state the rule -> fix one cause -> rerun the smallest failing case.

pages.content:
### Mastery review

Before moving on, you should be able to explain **JVM Memory, Garbage Collection and Performance** without looking at code, implement the smallest correct version, identify one edge case, and justify one API-design choice.

**Mastery checklist**
- [ ] Explain stack, heap and object lifetime at a practical level.
- [ ] Recognize allocation-heavy code patterns.
- [ ] Use simple measurements without confusing microbenchmarks with production profiling.

**Interview connection:** explain the feature in 30 seconds, give one runnable example, and name one failure mode or design trade-off.

**Transfer challenge:** change one requirement in the examples and predict what part of the implementation must change.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: Object lifetime
codeExamples.code: public class Main{static class Box{int x;Box(int x){this.x=x;}}public static void main(String[]a){Box b=new Box(42);System.out.println(b.x);b=null;System.out.println("eligible");}}
codeExamples.explanation: After the reference is removed, the object may become eligible for GC if unreachable from GC roots.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: StringBuilder allocation
codeExamples.code: public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){StringBuilder s=new StringBuilder();for(int i=0;i<5;i++)s.append(i);System.out.println(s);}}
codeExamples.explanation: StringBuilder avoids creating a new immutable String for every concatenation step.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: Simple timing
codeExamples.code: public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){long t=System.nanoTime();long s=0;for(int i=0;i<100000;i++)s+=i;long d=System.nanoTime()-t;System.out.println(s>0&&d>=0);}}
codeExamples.explanation: nanoTime can provide elapsed-time measurement, but reliable benchmarks need warm-up and repeated runs.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: Allocation hint
codeExamples.code: public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){String x="a"+1+2+3;System.out.println(x);}}
codeExamples.explanation: Compiler optimizations can reduce temporary allocations; inspect bytecode/profiling before assuming the cost.
